interview.hardest_part: The action economy versus real time. The clock keeps ticking while I think, and each turn is a single input, so a task like 'gather 3 cutgrass, gather 2 twigs, craft a torch, light it before dusk' costs a dozen or more turns of game time. Reading a small HUD from a single screenshot and converting it into a plan fast enough to matter is where the wheels come off. Nightfall is the sharpest edge of this: darkness kills in seconds, and it arrives at a fixed point no matter how slow I am.
interview.likely_failure: Dying on the first or second night because I mis-budgeted daylight and never got a torch or campfire down, or because I burned the day wandering and gathering without noticing the sky darkening. Secondary failure mode is standing still too long while chewing on a decision and starving, or accidentally attacking something I meant to gather.
interview.helpful_mechanics: Long Day stretches the safe window and the survival ladder is graded every 48 seconds, so just not dying pays out steadily rather than requiring a big win. The first-day area is dense with cutgrass, twigs, flint, berries and carrots, which converts cheaply into both collection points and the axe/pickaxe/torch/campfire craft points. Context-sensitive Space and hover labels mean I don't need pixel-perfect pointing to harvest. Cooking on a campfire and eating are also separate, cheap point categories.
interview.harmful_mechanics: Real-time continuation during thinking is the big one, and with only one attempt there's no rehearsal. Darkness is an instant loss condition with almost no grace period. The crafting bar is multi-step (tab, hover, click) and I have to re-locate it every screenshot. Hunger and sanity bars are small and easy to miss, combat against hounds or spiders is a coin flip given blind attack inputs, and the exotic collection items (silk, spidergland, pigskin, beefalowool, nitre, goldnugget) require either fights or structures I'm unlikely to reach in the time available.
